papers.title: Hypothalamic Orexin Neurons Modulate Sleep-Wake States and Seizure Burden in a Kainic Acid-Induced Mouse Model of Chronic Temporal Lobe Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sleep-wake states strongly influence seizure susceptibility, but the circuit mechanisms linking arousal regulation to seizure burden in chronic temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) remain unclear. This study investigated whether hypothalamic orexin neurons regulate sleep architecture, spontaneous seizures, and epileptic network activity in a kainic acid (KA)-induced chronic TLE model in male mice. Methods: Continuous video-EEG/EMG recordings were used to quantify sleep-wake states, circadian seizure distribution, and seizure burden. Orexin neurons were bidirectionally manipulated in KA-treated Hcrt-Cre mice using Cre-dependent hM3Dq or hM4Di chemogenetic tools. Orexin receptor 1 signaling was pharmacologically blocked with SB334867. Power spectral density and phase-amplitude coupling analyses were performed across wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement sleep, and rapid eye movement sleep. Results: Spontaneous seizures occurred predominantly during wakefulness and non-rapid eye movement sleep, with no seizures observed during rapid eye movement sleep. Seizure occurrence was greater during the dark phase and remained higher during wakefulness after correction for state occupancy. Chemogenetic activation of orexin neurons increased wakefulness, reduced sleep, and increased seizure count and total seizure duration, whereas chemogenetic inhibition produced opposite effects. SB334867 promoted sleep and reduced seizure count and total seizure duration. Chronic KA mice showed state-dependent spectral remodeling and enhanced delta-high-gamma coupling, which was partially attenuated by SB334867 during non-rapid eye movement and rapid eye movement sleep. Conclusions: These findings suggest that orexin signaling is associated with sleep-wake regulation, abnormal network coupling, and seizure burden in chronic TLE. Modulating orexin signaling may represent a potential direction for future therapeutic investigation aimed at improving sleep disruption and reducing seizure burden.

papers.title: A Temporally Causal Two-Layer Framework for Wearable EEG Sleep Staging and Short-Horizon Sleep-Transition Forecasting.
papers.abstract: Reliable online sleep monitoring requires sleep-stage estimates and forecasts based only on information available at the time of prediction. This study developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable electroencephalography (EEG) sleep staging and short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting. Using 128 Bitbrain Open Access Sleep (BOAS) recordings from 100 participants, the first layer (M0) performed five-stage sleep classification with causal signal processing and participant-isolated nested validation. The second layer (M1) used strictly cross-fitted histories of M0 stage probabilities to predict transitions from wake or N1 (W/N1) to N2, N3, or REM sleep (N2+) within 60, 90, or 120 s after each observed 30-s epoch. M1 eligibility was determined from M0-predicted stages during training and evaluation, without requiring polysomnography (PSG) stage labels at inference. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1. Under M0-predicted eligibility, M1 achieved AUROC values of 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s, respectively; complementary PSG-conditioned evaluation yielded 0.814, 0.803, and 0.801. Prediction was stronger during wakefulness than N1, and the benefits of probability history were specific to the future-sleep task. Future-perturbation tests confirmed unchanged pre-boundary outputs under the tested conditions. A frozen M0 replay on three Muse S Gen2 nights further identified stage-specific limitations in cross-device transfer. These findings establish an auditable framework for temporally causal wearable EEG analysis and demonstrate the potential of short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting while identifying its current generalization boundaries.

papers.title: Dihydromyricetin Regulates Sleep and Protects Against Oxidative Stress in Drosophila melanogaster.
papers.abstract: Sleep homeostasis is essential for health, and sleep disturbances contribute to multi-organ failure mortality. Dihydromyricetin (DMY), a flavonoid from Ampelopsis grossedentata, possesses anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. Although DMY alleviates sleep-deprivation-induced cognitive deficits, its role in sleep regulation remains unclear. Here, we show that DMY increases sleep duration and modulates sleep fragmentation in young, aged, and short-sleep mutant Drosophila. Transcriptomic and genetic analyses reveal that DMY alters the expression of neurotransmitter-related genes, including VGAT and Trhn, suggesting potential involvement of GABAergic and serotonergic signaling. In paraquat-induced oxidative stress models, DMY boosts antioxidant gene expression, alleviates oxidative damage and intestinal apoptosis, restores stress-disrupted sleep, and extends lifespan. Together, our findings demonstrate that DMY improves sleep-associated parameters, potentially involving neurotransmitter-related signaling pathways while concurrently mitigating oxidative stress-induced damage, thereby promoting organismal health and suggesting its potential for preventing and treating sleep disorders and aging-related decline.

papers.title: Sleep EEG distinguishes learned from novel auditory cues without predicting memory retention in a targeted memory reactivation study
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation during sleep is thought to build on processes initiated during encoding, but how encoding-related brain activity affects individual memories during sleep is unknown. Using targeted memory reactivation (TMR), we tested whether auditory cues elicit memory-related responses during sleep, whether encoding theta and delta power predict these responses, and whether encoding- and sleep-related measures predict long-term retention. Eighty-one healthy young adults learned sound-associated item-face/place pairs during electroencephalography (EEG). Memory was tested before sleep, 12 hours, and 5 days after encoding. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, a subset of learned sounds and novel control sounds were replayed. Item-level mixed-effects models assessed behavioural and EEG predictors of retention success, and item-level correlations related encoding to cue-induced power during sleep. Pre-sleep memory strength and encoding vividness predicted retention, with the vividness effect depending on encoding theta power. TMR did not improve memory and was associated with poorer retention of initially weak memories. Learned cues elicited stronger delta responses than novel sounds during sleep, yet cue-induced delta, theta, and sigma power did not predict retention. Encoding and sleep EEG power were unrelated and showed distinct scalp topographies. In a large item-level dataset, the sleeping brain distinguished learned from novel cues, but this processing did not translate into durable retention, which was instead determined at encoding. Encoding-related oscillations did not relate to memories preferentially reactivated or strengthened by sleep cueing. These findings caution against treating cue-induced sleep oscillations as markers of successful reactivation or consolidation.

papers.title: Alternative CLOCK isoforms specify a non-circadian timing circuit in Drosophila.
papers.abstract: Interval timing is a cognitive ability essential for behaviors such as mating, foraging, and decision-making, and it is distinct from circadian rhythm regulation. Despite the involvement of circadian clock genes in both interval timing and circadian rhythms, the mechanisms differentiating these functions remain unclear. Using Drosophila as a model, we indicate that CLOCK (CLK) and CYCLE (CYC), but not PERIOD (PER) and TIMELESS (TIM), are essential for interval timing. Neuronal CLK/CYC expression is required for sexual experience-dependent shorter mating duration (SMD) behavior. We identify a GAL4R54D11-positive clock-neuron population containing ion transport peptide-positive lateral dorsal neurons (ITP-LNd) and 5th small ventral lateral neurons (5th sLNv) as pivotal for SMD, with glutamatergic intersectional analyses pointing to ITP-LNd as the principal locus. Short CLK isoforms lacking the canonical DNA-binding motif are selectively required for SMD, whereas long- and short-isoform manipulations produce distinct effects on sleep duration. Our study uncovers a specialized circuit for interval timing and highlights the non-circadian functions of circadian clock genes.

papers.title: Phox2b 25-Ala expansion leads to Congenital Central Hypoventilation Syndrome like phenotypes in mice.
papers.abstract: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is a rare genetic disorder caused mainly by PHOX2B mutations and characterized by severe impairment of the autonomic nervous system and central control of breathing. The cardinal feature of CCHS is hypoventilation during sleep and an impaired hypercapnic ventilatory response. This defect has been linked, in part, to anatomical and functional abnormalities of phox2b-expressing neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), a key component of central CO₂ chemoreception. Although existing mouse models have provided major mechanistic insights, the severe and often perinatal phenotype of several models has limited their use for longer-term therapeutic testing. Here, we generated and characterized, for the first time, a new mouse model bearing the +5 alanine (+5Ala) expansion mutation (phox2b25Ala/+ mice) that reproduces CCHS-like phenotypes described in humans. Phox2b25Ala/+ pups suffered from hypoventilation and had a blunted response to hypercapnia at birth, leading to premature death in 75% of the pups. At the network level, the frequency of inspiratory activity in vitro was significantly reduced in phox2b25Ala/+ mice, and the response to acidosis was affected. At the cellular level, phox2b25Ala/+ mice had a reduced number of phox2b-expressing RTN neurons, with this reduction being less pronounced in the 25% of pups that survived. In conclusion, the +5 alanine expansion that causes CCHS reproduces CCHS-like phenotypes in mice. Phox2b25Ala/+ mice suffer from life-threatening hypoventilation that leads to premature death at birth and a lack of chemosensitivity. However, 25% of phox2b25Ala/+ mice survive until adulthood, representing a valuable opportunity for drug testing in CCHS.

papers.title: MG-STNet: A Compact Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Network for Adaptive Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging from polysomnography (PSG) is a core component of objective sleep analysis and plays a crucial role in enabling reliable clinical assessment and downstream physiological interpretation, yet the non-stationary nature of physiological signals poses significant challenges for compact models with fixed temporal receptive fields that cannot adapt to time-varying sleep rhythms. To address this challenge, we propose MG-STNet, a compact multi-granularity spatiotemporal network for adaptive sleep staging. The model first utilizes a Multi-Granularity Feature Learning Module (MFLM) to extract multi-resolution representations via parallel downsampling branches, thereby reducing sequence length and computational redundancy. Building on this compact representation, the Global-Local Feature Recalibration (GLFR) module recalibrates multi-channel PSG features by jointly leveraging global statistics and local temporal interactions, while the Adaptive Spatiotemporal Convolution (ASTC) module dynamically routes among complementary temporal branches to capture evolving sleep rhythms. Furthermore, a Temporal Attention Encoding Module (TAEM) is integrated to model long-range dependencies within each epoch. We evaluate MG-STNet on Sleep-EDF-20 and Sleep-EDF-78 using subject-independent k-fold cross-validation. The four-channel model achieves accuracies of 87.3% and 84.5% with 46.6K parameters and 17.2M FLOPs, while its single-channel counterpart achieves 86.6% and 83.2% with 48.6K parameters and 9.8M FLOPs. Experimental results indicate that MG-STNet achieves competitive accuracy with a substantially smaller parameter footprint than mainstream deep sleep-staging models, offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for automatic sleep staging under computational constraints.

papers.title: GamSleepNet: A Lightweight Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Based on Gabor Feature Extraction and Mamba Sequence Modeling for Single-Channel EEG.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging is a key technology for the precise diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders and for long-term home sleep monitoring. Due to its convenience of use, single-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) has become a research focus in home sleep monitoring. However, existing algorithms still face several practical bottlenecks. For example, models with a large number of parameters are prone to overfitting on small labeled datasets; the hardware heterogeneity of customized portable sensors makes datasets not directly shareable; large-scale labeled samples are hard to obtain in real scenarios; there is low recognition accuracy for difficult-to-distinguish sleep stages such as N1 and REM; and there is a lack of suitable research methods for evaluating the required scale of training data for lightweight deployment scenarios. In this paper we propose GamSleepNet, a low-parameter-count automatic sleep staging framework for single-channel EEG. The framework combines a feature extraction module (FEB), which integrates improved Gabor kernels with a learnable filter branch, with a standard Mamba selective state-space model (SSM) used for temporal modeling. A teacher-student feature alignment loss (FAL) and a two-stage training strategy are introduced to enhance the discriminative ability for difficult sleep stages. In addition, following the established paradigm of varying the training dataset's size and observing the performance curve, we make four adaptations tailored to sleep staging, thereby determining the appropriate training data volume for GamSleepNet and providing a methodological reference for determining the training data scale required for deploying other models. Under the limited-labeled-subject setting of the Sleep-EDF dataset, the model has 30.86 k parameters and achieves an overall accuracy of 87.86% and a macro F1 score of 82.62%-the highest values among the compared models-and improves the recognition of difficult REM and N1 samples. The model still maintains stable staging performance under low signal-to-noise ratio and label-scarce scenarios.

papers.title: Revisiting the First Night Effect of Polysomnography Using Wearable EEG Headbands in Older Adults with Sleep Disturbances
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: The first night effect (FNE), where sleep is altered during the first night of polysomnography (PSG), may affect the validity of single-night PSG assessments, yet its magnitude relative to habitual sleep is difficult to characterize using repeated PSG alone. We examined FNE during home-based PSG (HPSG) in older adults with sleep disturbances using multi-night wearable EEG headband (HB) recordings. Methods: Fifty-eight community-dwelling adults aged 55-85 years with sleep disturbances completed up to seven nights of HB monitoring, including one night of simultaneous HPSG. Using HB-derived measures, we compared total sleep time (TST), wake after sleep onset (WASO), sleep efficiency (SE), minutes in N3 sleep, and minutes in REM sleep between HPSG and non-HPSG nights via pairwise comparisons and linear mixed-effects models adjusting for age, sex, and race/ethnicity. Results: Sleep differed significantly between HPSG and non-HPSG nights, with roughly 35 minutes longer WASO, 21 minutes less N3 sleep, and 15% lower SE (ps < .001) during HPSG nights. TST and REM sleep did not differ between HPSG and non-HPSG nights. Findings were consistent when separately comparing nights preceding and following HPSG. Conclusions: In older adults with sleep disturbances, a single night of HPSG was associated with greater wake after sleep onset, less N3 sleep, and lower sleep efficiency than other nights measured with wearable EEG, suggesting that one-night PSG may overstate sleep disruption and understate deep sleep. Multi-night wearable EEG monitoring may help assess the representativeness of single-night PSG measurements, thereby improving the accuracy of sleep measurement interpretation.

papers.title: Fighting Sleep: Minute-by-Minute Driver Fatigue from a Dry-Electrode EEG Headband
papers.abstract: Driver-facing cameras often catch fatigue too late. We asked whether a four-electrode dry headband, which picks up eye movements electrically and head tilt with a motion sensor, can follow fatigue minute by minute. Nine participants wore the headband for twelve sessions of a 50-minute monotonous task at a driving simulator station, without driving, answering one cue a minute and rating their sleepiness every five minutes, with a webcam on the face for comparison. An index built without training from blink length, slow eye movements and head tilt, read against each participant's own first eight minutes, followed fatigue beyond elapsed time across the nine participants (0.32, p = 0.002), above zero in eight of them and at zero in the ninth. With its alarm line set for a 10 percent false-positive rate on not-sleepy minutes, it caught 91 percent of the minutes rated as fighting sleep, where the standard camera eye-closure measure (PERCLOS, the share of each minute with the eyes at least 80 percent closed), set the same way on the same minutes, caught 33 percent (67 minutes from four participants). Averaged over the six recordings that reached fighting sleep, the index crossed its alarm line about three minutes before the first minute rated as fighting sleep; in the five sessions with video its alarm had sounded by then in four, where the camera's sounded 6 to 13 minutes after in four and never in the fifth. The index and its alarm were then fixed and taken into a car, on one outing by one participant. Through a 33-minute rested drive the headband returned a value for every minute and raised no alarm. With the car parked and the driver doing the laboratory task, its alarm sounded nine minutes before he fell asleep, as seen on video; the camera's, set the same way, came eight minutes later, with one minute to spare. Signal amplitude at the electrodes was no higher in the parked car than in the laboratory, and with the car moving the electrodes that carry the index stayed in range 99 percent of the time.

papers.title: Preconditioning with Menaquinone-7 and Environmental Enrichment Produces Distinct Osteocalcin and Neuroplasticity Responses Following Chronic Social Defeat Stress.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Depression is a growing global health burden, underscoring the need for preventive strategies that complement existing treatments. Environmental enrichment (EE), incorporating physical, cognitive, sensory, and social stimulation, enhances neuroplasticity and stress resilience. Menaquinone-7 (MK-7), a form of vitamin K2, may also support brain health through osteocalcin, a bone-derived hormone involved in cognition and neuroplasticity. This study examined the protective effects of EE and MK-7 preconditioning, alone and combined, against chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), focusing on the osteocalcin-mediated bone-brain axis and structural plasticity. Materials and Methods: Male C57BL/6N mice received MK-7 (100 µg), EE, or both for four weeks before a 10-day CSDS protocol. Depressive-like behavior was assessed using the forced swim and tail suspension tests, while cognition was evaluated using novel object recognition and Y-maze tests. Serum osteocalcin, brain undercarboxylated osteocalcin (ucOC), brain gene expression of Bdnf, Gpr158, and Rbbp4, and protein levels of BDNF, MAP2, and GAP43 were measured. Results: CSDS induced depressive-like behavior and cognitive impairment, accompanied by reductions in serum and brain ucOC, Bdnf expression, BDNF, GAP43, and MAP2. Both MK-7 and EE showed significant main effects on behavioral and cognitive outcomes, while MK-7 exerted broader effects on osteocalcin- and neuroplasticity-related molecular markers. Significant MK-7 × EE interactions were limited to selected outcomes, including FST and brain ucOC, indicating outcome-specific rather than generalized synergy. Conclusions: CSDS disrupts the osteocalcin-mediated bone-brain axis and neuroplasticity-related pathways. MK-7 and EE both improved behavioral and cognitive outcomes, but MK-7 exerted broader effects on ucOC- and BDNF-related molecular markers, whereas their combination produced selective interactions rather than generalized synergy.

papers.title: Delayed Declarative and Procedural Memory Performance Following Interference: A Comparison of a 90-Min Midday Nap, Quiet Rest, and Active Wake.
papers.abstract: Newly formed memories are vulnerable to interference. Although sleep can stabilize memories and increase resistance to interference, whether quiet rest provides comparable delayed benefits remains unclear. This study compared the effects of a midday nap, quiet rest, and active wake on delayed declarative and procedural memory performance following interference learning. Post-interference performance served as the baseline. Thirty-seven habitual nappers (29 females and 8 males; mean age = 20.21 ± 3.04 years) were randomly assigned to nap (n = 13), quiet rest (n = 12), or active wake (n = 12) conditions, with polysomnography recorded during the assigned condition. Analyses of percentage change from the post-interference baseline revealed no significant group effects or group × time interactions for declarative or procedural memory. Procedural memory accuracy and speed showed greater improvement at next-day noon than in the evening. Exploratory Holm-corrected one-sample Wilcoxon tests showed improved procedural accuracy relative to the post-interference baseline in the nap group in the evening and in the nap and active wake groups at next-day noon, when speed improved in all three groups. These within-group changes do not establish between-group differences. In the nap group, frontal N2 slow spindle density was positively associated with next-day declarative memory accuracy, while slow spindle peak-phase coupling during N2 and N3 sleep was significantly associated with next-day changes in declarative memory accuracy. Greater REM sleep duration and percentage were associated with less improvement in evening procedural memory speed, whereas frontal N3 fast spindle phase-amplitude coupling was negatively associated with evening gains in procedural memory accuracy. No significant EEG-memory associations emerged during quiet rest. Overall, no significant nap-specific or quiet-rest behavioral advantage was detected. The EEG-memory associations were exploratory and do not establish a sleep-specific consolidation mechanism.

papers.title: A Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network with Context Gating for Frequency-Aware Sleep Stage Classification.
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep staging is important for assessing sleep architecture and supporting the diagnosis of sleep-related disorders. Manual scoring is time-consuming and subject to inter-scorer variability, while joint modeling of EEG channel relationships and frequency characteristics remains challenging. Methods: We propose DCMG-Net (dual-branch CNN and context-gated multi-view graph network), a frequency-aware network combining multi-view graph convolution with context gating for five-class sleep staging using EEG alone. Multiscale convolutions and attention extract channel features. Functional, globally learnable, and four physiological frequency-band adjacency matrices define six graph views, whose representations are adaptively fused by context gating. Results: On Sleep-EDF-20, ISRUC-S3, and the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS), overall accuracies were 91.2%, 90.0%, and 86.3%; macro-F1 scores were 84.4%, 88.7%, and 77.2%; and Cohen's κ values were 0.88, 0.87, and 0.81, respectively. Macro-F1 exceeded the highest values reported by the compared literature methods by 1.9, 4.2, and 0.7 percentage points, respectively. In the ablation experiments, gating improved macro-F1 over direct concatenation by 6.1 and 2.3 percentage points on ISRUC-S3 and SHHS. Conclusions: Frequency-band topology and context gating jointly exploit EEG frequency information and channel relationships to improve multi-view classification, providing a methodological basis for portable sleep monitoring and computer-assisted clinical scoring.

papers.title: Operational Definitions of Transition Onset Shape EEG Biomarker Timing in Drowsiness: A Single-Channel Method Comparison.
papers.abstract: Early-warning claims for electroencephalography (EEG)-based drowsiness detection rest on lead times, yet a lead time depends on how onset is operationally defined and is rarely tested against a null. We developed a benchmarking framework and applied it to seven onset estimators and 32 features from single-channel frontal EEG (17 participants, observer-verified drowsiness reports), with external replication in the DROZY dataset (13 sessions with an eligible vigilance-lapse anchor, of 20 retained). Estimator choice shifted onsets by minutes and changed detection coverage from 45% to 100% (Kendall's W = 0.53; external W = 0.71; absolute-agreement intraclass correlation 0.05). In simulation, two-standard-deviation baseline rules flagged onsets in 77-88% of no-change trajectories; null-calibrated thresholds (about 4.6 standard deviations) restored a nominal 5% rate. No estimator showed a statistically detectable excess of onsets in the final 150 s before the anchor relative to spectrum-preserving surrogates, a consensus detector fired before pseudo-anchors as often as before the true anchor, and adding EEG to elapsed session time gave no detectable improvement (area-under-the-curve difference 0.01, 95% confidence interval -0.11 to 0.13). Higuchi fractal dimension and line length correlated weakly with measured electrooculography (|r| ≤ 0.15). We propose interpretability criteria, evidence levels and a reporting checklist for early-onset claims.

papers.title: Exploratory Assessment of Portable EEG- and PPG-Derived Indices Following High-Intensity Exercise Under Partial Sleep Restriction in Young Men.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This exploratory study investigated associations between partial sleep restriction and portable device-derived prefrontal EEG and PPG indices, heart rate recovery (HRR), and perceived exertion (RPE) after high-intensity exercise in young men. Methods: Forty healthy men were randomly assigned to a normal sleep group (NSG; ~8 h, n = 20) or a sleep-restricted group (SRG; ~4 h, n = 20). Participants performed the Harvard Step Test (HST). Prefrontal EEG (Fp1 and Fp2) and single-site PPG were recorded for 1 min before and immediately after exercise using a portable consumer-grade device. Heart rate (HR), HRR, RPE, and physical fitness were assessed. Data were analyzed using mixed-design analysis of variance, t-tests, and supplementary linear mixed-effects models with Holm correction. Results: The theta-to-beta ratio (TBR) showed a significant group × time interaction (Holm-adjusted p = 0.034), increasing only in the SRG (p = 0.0014), whereas spectral edge frequency at 90% (SEF-90) showed no interaction (p = 0.781). Significant interactions were observed for the heart rate variability (HRV) index (p = 0.0085), sympathetic-related index (p < 0.001), and parasympathetic-related index (p = 0.0063). The HRV index decreased and the sympathetic-related index increased only in the SRG, whereas the parasympathetic-related index decreased in both groups. During recovery (1-3 min), the SRG had higher HR and lower HRR than the NSG (all p < 0.05). RPE was also higher in the SRG (p = 0.013). All reported p-values were Holm-adjusted. Conclusions: Partial sleep restriction was associated with changes in prefrontal EEG and exploratory PPG-derived indices, lower early HRR, and greater perceived exertion. The selective TBR response suggests index-dependent EEG changes. These findings warrant caution because of limited EEG spatial coverage, brief recordings, potential artifacts, and unvalidated proprietary algorithms. Device-derived changes do not directly establish altered central or autonomic neural activity.

papers.title: EEG Theta Power as an Indicator of Cognitive Workload in Student Pilots.
papers.abstract: Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4-8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. NASA-TLX results similarly indicated increased mental demand, effort, and frustration in the scenario associated with the highest cognitive workload. However, correlation analysis revealed a weak and inconsistent relationship between subjective workload ratings and EEG-derived theta measures across participants, with no clear or statistically significant overall association at the group level. These preliminary results indicate that scalp-recorded theta activity is sensitive to changes in task difficulty during flight simulation. However, given the exploratory nature of the study, the absence of flight-performance metrics, and the lack of strong correlation with subjective ratings, theta-band modulation should be interpreted as an index of task demand rather than a fully consolidated operational workload estimator.

papers.title: Neurocognitive and Behavioural Correlates of REM-Predominant Obstructive Sleep Apnoea.
papers.abstract: Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA, REM-OSA) is a phenotype in which obstructive respiratory events occur mainly during REM sleep, and may be associated with distinct daytime consequences. This study investigated the neurocognitive, behavioural, subjective sleep and polysomnographic profile of REM-OSA. Patients were classified as having REM-OSA when the REM Apnoea-Hypopnea Index (AHI)/Non-REM (NREM) AHI ratio was ≥ 2 and were compared with patients whose respiratory events predominantly occurred during NREM sleep (NREM-OSA). Patients evaluated for suspected OSA underwent a neuropsychological battery, including the Mini-Mental State Examination, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, Digit Span Forward/Backward, Trail Making Test (TMT), Frontal Assessment Battery and Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices, together with questionnaires evaluating sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale), impulsivity (Barratt Impulsiveness Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Of the 91 eligible patients, 17 had mild OSA and were included in sensitivity analyses, while the primary analysis included 74 patients with moderate-to-severe OSA. Thirteen (17.6%) met REM-OSA criteria, and 61 were classified as NREM-OSA. REM-OSA patients had lower overall AHI and oxygen desaturation index and, after False Discovery Rate correction, longer TMT-A, TMT-B and TMT B-A (all q = 0.003). After adjustment for depressive symptoms, REM-OSA independently predicted longer TMT-A (β = 0.298, p = 0.002), TMT-B (β = 0.235, p = 0.016), TMT B-A (β = 0.258, p = 0.018) and higher impulsivity (β = 0.237, p = 0.043), but not global PSQI scores (β = 0.210, p = 0.086). Sensitivity analyses confirmed poorer TMT-A performance in REM-OSA. These results highlight the neurocognitive relevance of REM phenotype despite lower overall respiratory severity.

papers.title: tACS and nervonic acid inhibit microglial overactivation via the Rap1 signaling pathway and ameliorate sleep deprivation-induced cognitive impairment.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) has become a critical global health concern, with consequences including cognitive decline. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) holds significant potential for improving cognitive impairment. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of tACS on SD-associated cognitive deficits. Male C57BL/6 mice were subjected to SD using the horizontal platform method. Cognitive function was assessed via multiple behavioral tests, and local field potential (LFP) signals were recorded. Untargeted metabolomics was employed to identify key metabolites and regulatory pathways in mouse brain tissue. Mouse models and co-culture systems were combined to investigate the regulatory relationships among microglia, synapses, and neurons. tACS significantly improved memory and cognitive function in SD-induced model mice, accompanied by inhibited microglial phagocytosis, increased synaptic density, and reduced neuronal apoptosis. Untargeted metabolomics revealed that tACS may regulate nervonic acid (NA) abundance and the Rap1 signaling pathway during SD. Further studies demonstrated that NA suppresses lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced microglial overactivation and synaptic loss via the Rap1 signaling pathway, thereby blocking neuronal apoptosis. Additionally, similar to the therapeutic effects of tACS, NA administration markedly alleviated cognitive impairment and neural damage in SD mice. These data support the regulatory roles of tACS and NA in neuronal activity and synaptic plasticity and propose novel therapeutic targets for SD-related cognitive deficits.

papers.title: Objective-to-Subjective Sleep Discrepancy in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Pilot EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Sleep disturbance is common in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the relationship between subjectively perceived and objectively measured sleep duration remains poorly understood. This pilot study aimed to compare objective and subjective total sleep time (TST) and to explore clinical factors associated with each measure and the difference between them. It also examined the relationship between this difference and nocturnal blood pressure regulation. Materials and Methods: Twenty-two hospitalized patients with RA underwent overnight sleep monitoring using a portable single-channel electroencephalography (EEG) device and provided subjective estimates of TST for the same night in response to a question asked the following morning. Sleep discrepancy was defined as subjective minus EEG-derived TST. Associations with clinical variables were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction. Exploratory regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index were performed. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was available for 20 patients. Results: Subjective TST exceeded EEG-derived TST by a median of 82.75 min (p = 0.0008), and the two measurements were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.119, p = 0.598). A more positive signed sleep discrepancy was associated with lower serum albumin (ρ = -0.723, q = 0.0020), higher C-reactive protein (CRP) levels (ρ = 0.624, q = 0.0134), glucocorticoid use (q = 0.0462), higher DAS28-CRP (q = 0.0495), and greater functional disability (q = 0.0495). Associations with albumin and CRP persisted in separate exploratory models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Patients with a conventional dipper blood pressure (BP) pattern had a lower signed sleep discrepancy than those with other nocturnal BP patterns (p = 0.0087). Conclusions: In this small exploratory study, subjective sleep duration in patients with RA was generally longer than EEG-derived sleep duration. Furthermore, preliminary associations were observed between sleep discrepancy and inflammatory and clinical characteristics, as well as with nocturnal BP patterns. These findings require confirmation in larger studies, and the clinical significance of sleep discrepancy remains uncertain.

papers.title: Evaluating Autonomic and Cognitive Responses to Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation as a Countermeasure for Sleep Deprivation.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute sleep deprivation impairs cognitive performance in safety-critical occupations, highlighting a demand for effective countermeasures. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has been explored as an alternative noninvasive neuromodulatory approach to mitigating performance decline. Groups have also capitalized on the ability of biosignals like heart rate variability (HRV) to continuously track performance decline during extended wakefulness, but whether fatigue interventions like tDCS shift the autonomic measures used in such tracking during sleep deprivation remains unknown. This study examined whether tDCS affects autonomic function and cognitive performance during sleep deprivation. Methods: Nineteen participants underwent 26 h of continuous wakefulness with repeated cognitive assessments and electrocardiogram monitoring. After 19 h awake, participants received 30 min of verum (n = 10) or sham (n = 9) tDCS targeting the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in a double-blind design. Performance and HRV were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction, including 5 min windowed analyses of the Multi-Attribute Task Battery-II (MATB). Results: Stimulation had no significant main effect on any cognitive performance or HRV outcome. Exploratory analyses revealed stimulation × window interactions within the MATB for system monitoring reaction time, resource management performance, and absolute high-frequency HRV power. Verum participants reported lower sleepiness at a single post-stimulation round without a corresponding performance benefit. Conclusions: In this exploratory sample, a single tDCS session produced no detectable group-level effects on cognitive performance or HRV, and apart from one exploratory within-task interaction, no systematic stimulation-related shift in autonomic measures was observed. Effect size estimates and exploratory findings within tasks provide a basis for adequately powered studies examining individual variability in tDCS response.

papers.title: Visual function and circadian rest-activity rhythms in US older adults: The National Health and Aging Trends Study.
papers.abstract: To evaluate associations of visual function with accelerometer-derived rest-activity rhythm (RAR) metrics and 24-hour continuous activity patterns among older adults. We analyzed data from 728 U.S. Medicare beneficiaries (weighted mean age 79.1±6.0 years, 78% White, 56% female) who completed objective vision assessments and provided ≥ 3 days of accelerometer data in NHATS Round 11 (2021). Visual functions included distance acuity, near acuity, and contrast sensitivity. Wrist-worn accelerometer data were used to derive parametric RAR metrics (amplitude, mesor, acrophase, alpha, beta, and percent rhythm) and nonparametric RAR metrics (relative amplitude, intradaily variability [IV], interdaily stability [IS]). Associations were examined using weighted linear regression and function-on-scalar regression (FOSR). Poorer visual function, regardless of type, was associated with lower amplitude (rhythm strength, both parametric and non-parametric metrics) and lower percent rhythm (rhythmicity), but not with mesor (average activity level), acrophase (peak activity timing), or alpha (peak-trough width). Distance acuity showed a statistically significant nonlinear association with IS. We did not observe any statistically significant associations for beta and IV after type 1 error correction. FOSR showed lower daytime activity and higher nighttime activity during typical sleep hours among those with vision impairment, with simultaneous significance limited to a small portion of the day. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Worse visual function was associated with weaker and less robust circadian RARs in a representative sample of older adults. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies are warranted to understand the intertwined relationships between visual function and circadian health.

papers.title: Short-video addiction and circadian phase delay in Chinese adolescents and emerging adults: A three-wave longitudinal study with a nested dim-light melatonin assessment.
papers.abstract: To examine whether short-video addiction is longitudinally associated with endogenous circadian phase delay in Chinese youth, and whether health behaviors mediate this association differently across educational stages and genders. In a 3-wave longitudinal cohort of 1660 students (520 middle-school, 610 high-school, 530 university), short-video use was logged objectively and saliva was sampled at 23:00 on 3 nights per wave; a nested subsample (n = 120) completed overnight dim-light melatonin assessments each wave, enabling calibrated phase-delay estimation (intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.89). The proportion in the Short Video Addiction Scale (SVAS)-defined high-score range rose across educational stages (18.3%, 27.7%, 36.4%). The phase-delay association per standard deviation of addiction strengthened from middle school to university (0.92 vs. 2.15 hours; ratio 2.34, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.8-3.1). In the extreme-groups laboratory subsample (n = 120; SVAS ≥ 31 vs. ≤ 15), health behaviors statistically mediated 65.7% (95% CI 58.3%-72.1%) of the total association-an estimate that applies to these selected extreme groups, with its magnitude across the full exposure distribution remaining uncertain; the dominant pathway shifted from physical activity (middle school) to sleep quality and diet (high school) to psychological stress (university), with educational-stage-dependent gender differences. A nighttime-use breakpoint near 90 minutes was internally consistent across all 3 waves and requires external validation; educational-stage-specific breakpoints and educational stage × gender pathway differences are hypothesis-generating. Short-video addiction is associated with circadian phase delay through educational-stage- and gender-specific behavioral pathways. Findings are associational and support tailored prevention research.

papers.title: Quantitative EEG Differences Across Two Sedation Conditions in a Child with Epilepsy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Sedation is frequently required to obtain electroencephalography (EEG) recordings in children with neurodevelopmental disorders and structural etiologies of epilepsy. However, the extent to which different sedative agents influence quantitative interictal epileptiform discharge (IED) burden remains insufficiently characterized. A child with congenital cytomegalovirus-associated structural brain injury underwent EEG recordings under two sedation conditions: continuous low-dose propofol infusion and oral chloral hydrate. Quantitative analyses were performed using a duration-matched, within-subject design. Artifact-minimized EEG segments of equal duration (15.52 min) were analyzed. IED burden was quantified using spike frequency (spikes/min) and spike index (percentage of 10 s epochs containing ≥1 spike). Spectral power distribution and spectral edge frequency (SEF95) were also evaluated. The chloral hydrate recording showed a higher observed spike frequency than the propofol recording (14.11 vs. 4.12 spikes/min; descriptive rate ratio, 3.42) and a higher 10-s spike index (84.95% vs. 27.96%). Spectral analysis demonstrated lower SEF95 and greater delta predominance in the propofol recording, whereas the chloral hydrate recording showed relatively greater theta-alpha activity. The two recordings showed marked differences in apparent IED burden and background spectral characteristics. However, because they were obtained approximately one year apart and under different clinical circumstances, including intercurrent illness during the chloral hydrate recording, these differences cannot be attributed specifically to the sedative agents. This case illustrates the importance of considering sedation, clinical context, and vigilance state when longitudinally interpreting quantitative pediatric EEG findings.

papers.title: Guipi Tang Combined with Probiotics Ameliorates Sleep Deprivation-Induced Hippocampal Injury and Pentobarbital-Induced Sleep Alterations in Mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance is a prevalent health problem associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis, chronic inflammation, and neuronal dysfunction. Here, we show that Guipi Tang (GPT) combined with probiotics is associated with improvements in pentobarbital-induced sleep responses and hippocampal injury in mice. Compared with individual treatments, the combined intervention showed improvements in several measured outcomes and was associated with changes in gut microbial composition, inflammatory markers, and hippocampal injury. 16S rRNA (16S ribosomal RNA) sequencing (n = 5 per group) revealed alterations in gut microbial composition following sleep deprivation, while the combined treatment modulated the relative abundance of several bacterial taxa. Furthermore, serum levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor-alpha) and IL-1β (interleukin-1 beta) differed significantly among groups (n = 5 per group; F (4,20) = 3.959, p = 0.0159 and F (4,20) = 10.26, p = 0.0001, respectively). Western blot analysis (n = 4 per group) revealed significant differences in the expression of autophagy-related markers, including ATG5 (F (4,15) = 8.319, p = 0.0032), Beclin-1 (F (4,15) = 13.62, p < 0.0001), the LC3-II (F (4,15) = 13.56, p < 0.0001), and p62 (F (4,15) = 5.870, p = 0.0048). Compared with the Model group, combined treatment significantly increased ATG5, LC3-II and Beclin-1 expression, while reducing p62 expression. In addition, the Bcl-2/Bax ratio increased significantly following combined treatment (n = 4 per group, p < 0.01 vs. Model), accompanied by a reduction in TUNEL-positive cells. Changes in Akt phosphorylation were also observed, although the relationship between Akt signaling and autophagy requires further investigation. Collectively, these findings suggest that GPT combined with probiotics is associated with improvements in pentobarbital-induced sleep responses and hippocampal injury in sleep-deprived mice, accompanied by changes in gut microbial composition, inflammatory markers, and Akt-associated autophagy-related signaling.

papers.title: Chronic Sleep Deprivation-Induced Anxiety-Like Behaviors Correlate With Altered Peripheral S100A10+ Immune Cells and Hippocampal Metabolic Dysregulation.
papers.abstract: To characterize biological alterations associated with chronic sleep deprivation (CSD)-related anxiety-like behaviors in mice and to explore the parallel association between peripheral immunity and central metabolism. A mouse model of CSD was established by subjecting mice to 7 days of sleep deprivation. Anxiety-like behaviors were evaluated using the open field test (OFT) and elevated plus maze (EPM) test. Peripheral blood immune cell subsets and S100A10 levels were analyzed using flow cytometry. Blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity and inflammatory levels in peripheral blood and hippocampal tissues were assessed through immunofluorescence staining, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR). Hippocampal metabolic profiles were characterized using untargeted metabolomics. Intrinsic interactions among behavioral, immune, and metabolic indices were evaluated through correlation analysis. The functional pathways associated with the differential metabolites were determined using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis. CSD mice exhibited typical anxiety-like behaviors, characterized by reduced time spent in the central area in the OFT and fewer entries into that area, as well as increased latency to enter the open arms in the EPM test. At the peripheral immune level, CSD did not alter the proportions of total T cells or total monocytes. However, the proportion of proinflammatory Ly6C+ high monocytes increased, whereas that of anti-inflammatory Ly6C+ low monocytes decreased. CSD disrupted the BBB, promoted microglial activation, and elevated proinflammatory cytokine concentrations in the peripheral blood and hippocampal tissue. Furthermore, CSD upregulated S100A10 expression in CD45+ leukocytes, CD8+ T cells, and total monocytes. At the hippocampal metabolome level, CSD induced 157 differential metabolites. The levels of metabolites including ginsenoyne K were significantly upregulated, while those of metabolites such as phosphatidylinositol were downregulated. Additionally, multiple metabolites were associated with core anxiety-related behavioral parameters. KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that differential metabolites were primarily enriched in neurofunction-related pathways, including the cAMP-signaling pathway and glutathione metabolism. Correlation analysis further unveiled that the proportion of peripheral T cells, the balance between monocyte subsets, S100A10 levels in total monocytes, and key hippocampal metabolites were closely associated with anxiety-like behaviors. CSD induces anxiety-like behaviors in mice, it alters the distribution of peripheral monocyte subsets, upregulates S100A10 levels in specific immune cells, and remodels hippocampal metabolism. Moreover, CSD disrupts BBB integrity and activates microglia in the hippocampus.

papers.title: Self-generated action shapes theta phase alignment at encoding and later recollection
papers.abstract: Across species, self-directed action is linked to theta rhythms and better memory, but such action combines choosing, moving, and controlling the outcome. Whether choosing and control over the outcome shape recollection, and the encoding dynamics that support it, remains unclear. Three preregistered experiments in human participants separated these components while holding movement constant. Participants encoded scene pairs by dragging either a freely chosen scene or one indicated by the program, with fluent or disrupted feedback. Recognition was tested after 24 hours (and immediately in Experiment 2), using Remember/Know judgments. Experiment 3 recorded scalp electroencephalography during encoding. Choosing improved recognition, more for recollection than familiarity. A smaller benefit extended to the unselected scene, although less consistently after latency adjustment. Disrupted feedback lowered rated agency but did not reduce memory at 24 hours. In Experiment 2, however, recollection declined less over 24 hours after self-generated than externally generated action, but only under fluent feedback. Choosing increased action-onset-locked theta and alpha phase alignment (inter-trial phase coherence), whereas disrupted feedback reduced alignment later. The selection effects survived matching for response-initiation-latency. Trial by trial, later posterior theta alignment (353-570 ms) predicted Remember over Know responses, whereas early frontal alpha alignment (127-245 ms) predicted Remember over Forgotten responses. These findings link self-generated action to the timing of encoding-related oscillations and to subsequent recollection. The association between later posterior theta alignment and Remember-Know discrimination is consistent with a role for theta phase coordination in associative binding.

papers.title: Circadian Disruption and the 24-Hour Blood Pressure Phenotype in Arterial Hypertension.
papers.abstract: Arterial hypertension is not only a disorder of blood pressure level but also of its temporal organization. This review examines circadian disruption as a multidimensional determinant of the hypertensive phenotype and proposes the 24 h blood pressure profile as an integrated downstream physiological phenotype rather than a direct measure of intrinsic clock dysfunction. Nocturnal hypertension, non-dipping, reverse dipping, morning blood pressure transition, and short-term variability are related but non-equivalent phenotypes with different determinants and imperfect reproducibility. Controlled human studies support causal effects of acute circadian misalignment on selected cardiovascular and metabolic processes, whereas free-living evidence is predominantly observational and confounded by coexisting sleep, metabolic, occupational, and behavioral exposures. Emerging evidence on sleep regularity, social jetlag, nighttime light, meal timing, and time-restricted eating identifies potentially modifiable pathways, but their independent contribution remains difficult to separate from energy balance, weight loss, sleep, and behavioral regularity. Randomized trials do not support universal bedtime antihypertensive dosing. We therefore frame circadian-informed hypertension care around multidimensional phenotyping, with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring as the established cardiovascular output and upstream sleep, behavioral, metabolic, environmental, and, where feasible, endogenous circadian measures. The key translational question is whether reproducible temporal phenotypes can guide interventions that improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes beyond conventional hypertension management.

Demographic files included 32 patients with MS and 32 healthy controls (HC); global-feature models included 29 patients with MS and 32 HC, and channel-level sample sizes varied by feature. Diagnosis and age were entered in linear models. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied separately to five global spectral/aperiodic tests, 16 global microstate tests, and the 128 channel-wise tests within each feature. Within-MS continuous age regression and exploratory age-stratified ANOVA were evaluated with the same family definitions. No within-MS continuous-age or age-stratified result survived FDR correction. Aperiodic offset showed the strongest diagnosis association under the specified age-adjusted model. However, the MS and HC age ranges did not overlap (21-55 vs. 56-83 years), so the diagnosis coefficient depends on extrapolation and cannot establish an MS-specific effect. papers.title: Zhibai Anshen Oral Liquid Activates cAMP/PKA/CREB Signaling Axis and Promotes BDNF and Circadian Clock Protein Expression to Ameliorate Insomnia.
papers.abstract: Zhibai Anshen oral liquid (ZBAS) was optimized from classical traditional Chinese medicine formula Zhimubaihe decoction, and it has been approved for clinical treatment of insomnia for over 30 years, achieving a satisfying effect. However, its potential mechanisms are still unclear. This study aims to uncover the key mechanisms of ZBAS in ameliorating insomnia-like behaviors. Insomnia rats were established, and the effect of ZBAS on insomnia was assessed. Histological assessments via H&E and Nissl staining were conducted to evaluate the pathological alterations in the hippocampus, while the regulatory effects of ZBAS on neurotransmitters (5-HT, GABA, and NE) were simultaneously determined. To assess neuronal viability in rats, we monitored NeuN expression via immunofluorescence staining, alongside the quantification of circadian clock proteins (PER3 and CLOCK). Furthermore, network pharmacology was coupled with RNA-seq to filter key molecules of ZBAS against insomnia. To thoroughly substantiate the pivotal signaling networks mapped out by KEGG pathway enrichment, complementary in vivo assays were subsequently conducted. Our findings showed that ZBAS effectively counteracted insomnia-driven weight loss, while concurrently reducing sleep latency and extending total sleep duration in rats. These behavioral improvements were accompanied by enhanced neuronal viability and elevated levels of circadian clock proteins. A total of 151 potential targets of ZBAS in ameliorating insomnia were identified through RNA-seq and network pharmacology analysis. PPI analysis revealed that BDNF was a key molecule. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that the amelioration of insomnia by ZBAS was closely related to the cAMP signaling pathway. Further results suggested that the ameliorative effect of ZBAS on insomnia-like behaviors in PCPA-induced rats was associated with activation of the cAMP/PKA/CREB axis and was accompanied by upregulation of BDNF and circadian clock proteins. Notably, MDL12330A (an adenylyl cyclase inhibitor) attenuated the ameliorative effects of ZBAS on insomnia. This study provides evidence that, in PCPA-induced insomnia rats, cAMP/PKA/CREB signaling contributes to the anti-insomnia effect of ZBAS, which is associated with upregulation of BDNF and circadian clock proteins; however, whether the upregulation of BDNF and PER3/CLOCK is required for the anti-insomnia effect remains to be experimentally verified.

papers.title: Sex-Stratified Associations Between Sleep-Stage-Specific Respiratory Indices and Metabolic Parameters in Children with Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: To examine whether sex modifies associations between whole-night and sleep-stage-specific respiratory indices and metabolic parameters in children with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This retrospective cross-sectional secondary analysis included a previously reported cohort of 514 children (330 boys, 184 girls) referred for suspected sleep-disordered breathing. Whole-night, rapid eye movement (REM), and non-rapid eye movement (NREM) obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI) and oxygen desaturation index (ODI) were examined in sex-stratified and pooled interaction models adjusted for age and body mass index z-score. Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied across 30 interaction tests. Sleep architecture was also assessed. After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, triglycerides (TG) were positively associated with all six respiratory indices in both sexes. Sex interactions were significant for TG with whole-night OAHI (standardized β = -0.509; 95% CI, -0.737 to -0.281) and NREM OAHI (β = -0.582; 95% CI, -0.813 to -0.350; both q < 0.001), indicating stronger associations in girls (boys minus girls). No other interactions survived FDR correction. Sex-related heterogeneity was confined to selected TG-OAHI associations. Independent prospective validation is needed to assess reproducibility and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Immediate responses to stimulation of trigeminal-associated sites using conventional suction-type and wearable silicone SSP electrodes: An exploratory randomized three-arm study in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: BackgroundComparative evidence regarding the immediate subjective and physiological responses to conventional suction-type and wearable conductive silicone silver spike point (SSP) electrodes remains limited.ObjectiveTo compare responses to conventional SSP stimulation at V1-associated sites and wearable silicone SSP stimulation at V3-associated sites with a nonequivalent no-current control.MethodsFifty-four healthy young adults were randomized to control, conventional SSP, or silicone SSP groups (18 per group). Conventional electrodes were applied without current in the control group, whereas both active groups received 20 min of stimulation. The primary outcome was pre-to-post change in the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS). Exploratory secondary outcomes included electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate variability (HRV), and masseter electromyography (EMG). Analyses included mixed repeated-measures ANOVA and Welch ANOVA with Dunnett T3-adjusted comparisons.ResultsA significant time × group interaction was observed for KSS [F(2, 51) = 4.693, p = .013, partial η2 = .155]. Mean ± SD changes were 0.53 ± 1.77, 1.14 ± 1.95, and 2.92 ± 3.28 points in the control, conventional SSP, and silicone SSP groups, respectively. Post hoc analysis showed a significant difference between the silicone SSP and control groups (mean difference, 2.389; 95% CI, 0.154-4.624; adjusted p = .034), but not between the two active stimulation groups (adjusted p = .162). No significant time × group interactions were observed for EEG, HRV, or EMG.ConclusionKSS changes differed between silicone SSP and no-current control, but superiority or equivalence relative to conventional SSP was not established. The simultaneous differences in stimulation site and electrode design prevent attribution of the observed findings to either factor independently.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture Ameliorates Circadian Rhythm Disruption-Induced Oligoasthenospermia in Mice by Modulating the Sirt1/Nrf2 Antioxidant Signaling Pathway.
papers.abstract: The growing prevalence of shift work and nocturnal light exposure in modern lifestyles has made circadian disruption an underrecognized environmental risk factor for male oligoasthenospermia. The core molecular network underlying circadian disruption-induced spermatogenic impairment remains incompletely understood, and targeted non-pharmacological interventions are limited. This study sought to identify candidate regulatory targets for circadian disruption-related oligoasthenospermia and investigate the protective mechanism of electroacupuncture. Gene sets associated with circadian rhythm and oligoasthenospermia were retrieved from GeneCards, OMIM, and GEO databases. Candidate hub genes and pathways were screened via intersection analysis, functional enrichment, and seven machine learning algorithms. A chronic jet lag mouse model was established and randomly divided into control, circadian disruption, and electroacupuncture groups. Sperm parameters, serum reproductive hormone levels, testicular and hepatic clock gene expression, testicular histology, oxidative stress status, and Sirt1/Nrf2 pathway activity were assessed. Five hub genes linked to both circadian rhythm and oligoasthenospermia (IL1B, NFE2L2, PCNA, DMPK, MYH9) were identified, with functional enrichment highlighting pathways related to oxidative stress, gonadal development, and hormone regulation. In vivo, circadian disruption impaired sperm quality, dysregulated reproductive hormones, downregulated testicular clock genes, disrupted spermatogenic structure, elevated testicular oxidative stress, and suppressed the Sirt1/Nrf2 pathway. Electroacupuncture effectively reversed these pathological changes, restored hepatic clock rhythmicity, and upregulated key molecules of the testicular Sirt1/Nrf2 antioxidant pathway. Electroacupuncture ameliorates circadian disruption-induced spermatogenic impairment in mice. This protective effect is associated with the restoration of peripheral circadian rhythm and activation of the testicular Sirt1/Nrf2 antioxidant pathway.

papers.title: Effects of Intermittent Theta-Burst Stimulation over the Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex on Executive Function During Sustained Simulated Flight Operations: A Randomized Crossover Study Using a Flight-Cognitive Dual-Task Paradigm.
papers.abstract: Sustained flight operation load may compromise executive control in complex human-machine interaction environments. Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) holds potential for modulating executive function, yet its effects on different executive components under sustained operational load remain unclear. This study employed a randomized, balanced, within-subject crossover design, enrolling 25 healthy male participants. Each participant completed three intervention conditions: Active iTBS, Sham iTBS, and No-stimulation. Each experimental session consisted of stimulation delivery, a 60-min cruising simulated flight, and a 30-min flight-cognitive dual-task phase. Primary outcomes were behavioral performance on the Go/No-Go, 3-back, and number-rule switching tasks; EEG microstates and prefrontal relative oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) changes during the dual-task phase served as exploratory neurophysiological indices. Results showed that condition differences were concentrated in working memory updating and rule switching: compared with No-stimulation, Active iTBS shortened 3-back reaction time and reduced switch cost; compared with both No-stimulation and Sham iTBS, Active iTBS improved 3-back accuracy and number-rule switching accuracy; the switch-cost difference between Active and Sham iTBS did not reach significance (pBonferroni = 0.055). No significant condition effect was observed for the Go/No-Go task. EEG microstate analysis revealed task-specific changes: under the Active iTBS condition, the occurrence rate and temporal coverage of microstate D increased during the 3-back task; temporal coverage of microstate D increased during the number-rule switching task; no significant microstate changes were observed during the Go/No-Go task. Exploratory fNIRS analysis indicated that left-hemisphere and all-channel prefrontal HbO under Active iTBS was higher than under Sham iTBS in planned pairwise comparisons (pBonferroni < 0.03), but the corresponding condition main effects (p ≥ 0.065) and condition × hemisphere interaction (p = 0.919) were non-significant, and channel-level effects did not survive multiple-comparison correction. These findings suggest that, within the flight-cognitive dual-task paradigm, Active iTBS over the left DLPFC is associated with improvements in working memory and rule switching performance, accompanied by changes in microstate temporal organization during certain tasks. The microstate and fNIRS results provide exploratory neurophysiological observations and cannot establish causal relationships with the behavioral improvements.

papers.title: Detecting cognitive motor dissociation in unresponsive brain-injured patients: a prospective cohort study using active task-based EEG.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to assess the prevalence and prognostic value of cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) detected by active task-based electroencephalography (EEG) in a cohort of patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC). In a prospective cohort study, we enrolled 56 consecutive clinically unresponsive patients with acute or chronic brain injury. Patients underwent EEG recording during an active motor imagery task following spoken commands. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOS-E) at 6 months. Ten healthy volunteers served as a control group. Among the 56 unresponsive patients, 6 (10.7%) were identified as CMD-positive. The favorable-outcome rate (GOS‑E ≥ 4) was higher in the CMD-positive group (2/6, 33.3%) than in the CMD-negative group (4/50, 8.0%), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (Fisher's exact p = 0.12). At 6‑month follow‑up, no deaths occurred in the CMD‑positive group (n = 6), compared with a mortality rate of 16% (8/50) in the CMD‑negative group. Given the limited sample size, these descriptive results are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger prospective cohorts. In the healthy control group, 9 of 10 participants (90%) were task‑positive; the only task‑negative participant reported having fallen asleep during the experiment. Most healthy volunteers reported feeling drowsy and easily distracted while performing the task. Active task‑based EEG can detect CMD in a subset of behaviorally unresponsive patients, and its presence was descriptively associated with more favorable outcomes. However, the detection rate in our cohort was lower than previously reported, and healthy controls frequently experienced sleepiness during the task. These findings support the prognostic value of EEG‑detected CMD while highlighting the need for more sensitive, patient‑adapted paradigms.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythms, Exercise, and Metabolic Remodeling in MASLD: From Chronometabolism to Muscle-Preserving Care.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) links hepatic lipid accumulation with insulin resistance, disturbed sleep, and impaired muscle health. This critical narrative review integrates clinical, metabolomics, and mechanistic evidence identified through a structured multi-database search and citation-tracing workflow covering PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar to 30 September 2026, focusing on circadian regulation, exercise, and muscle-preserving care. Hepatic clocks coordinate nutrient handling, bile-acid signaling, mitochondrial metabolism, and redox balance. Sleep and meal-timing disruption are associated with adverse metabolic phenotypes, although MASLD-specific causal evidence remains limited. Exercise improves liver and metabolic outcomes, but no universal optimal session time has been established. Time-restricted eating should be evaluated alongside energy intake, diet quality, protein distribution, sleep, and adherence. Complex lipids, acylcarnitines, bile acids, ketone bodies, and amino acids offer complementary research signals; their interpretation requires standardized sampling, analytical quality control, and external validation. Circulating concentrations should not be equated with tissue flux or treatment benefit. Clinical care should integrate fibrosis and cardiometabolic risk assessment with sustainable weight management, progressive resistance and aerobic exercise, adequate protein, and sleep assessment. Future trials should pair repeated, timed metabolite measurements with liver, body-composition, strength, and physical-function outcomes to establish whether these signatures improve clinical decisions.

papers.title: EEG morphology and peri-ictal MRI abnormalities in status epilepticus and ictal-interictal continuum.
papers.abstract: Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency that may have long-term consequences. Peri-ictal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities (PMAs) may serve as marker of potential acute ictal brain injury and can be used for estimating the risk of SE-defining electroencephalography (EEG) patterns. We hypothesized that excitatory-predominant EEG morphologies reflect higher metabolic demand and a greater likelihood of PMAs than inhibitory-predominant morphologies. In this single-center prospective cohort (February 2019-April 2025), we included patients who had either SE or ictal-interictal continuum (IIC) reported on EEG and underwent acute magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (≤48 h). Excitatory-predominant morphology was defined by a sharp-wave amplitude greater than those of the positive and slow wave, a broad sharp wave (>200 ms), or superimposed fast activity. Inhibitory-predominant morphology was defined by the positive or slow-wave amplitude greater than that of a sharp wave. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between EEG morphology and PMAs on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho assessed correlations between the number of excitatory features (0-2) and MRI sequences showing PMAs (none, arterial spin labeling [ASL] hyperperfusion only, or DWI/FLAIR). Among 205 included patients (134 IIC, 71 SE), excitatory-predominant patterns and lateralized periodic discharges were associated with increased risk of DWI/FLAIR PMAs (p = .001 and p = .02, respectively). In IIC patients, excitatory-predominant morphology was the only predictor of PMAs (p = .002). In the subset with ASL, DWI, and FLAIR sequences (n = 145), the number of excitatory features correlated strongly with types of sequences affected by PMAs (Kendall's tau p < .001; Spearman's rho p < .001). Excitatory-predominant morphology, as opposed to inhibitory-predominant patterns, was associated with a more frequent occurrence of PMAs. These findings support an EEG morphology framework based on excitatory-inhibitory balance across IIC and SE.

papers.title: From hemodynamics to function: the role of fNIRS and hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems in next-generation assistive technologies for rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Assistive technologies (AT) serve as fundamental tools for rehabilitation because they help people with neurological or physical disabilities to restore their abilities, independence and their overall life satisfaction. Existing AT control methods, which include manual operation, eye tracking, voice commands, electromyography (EMG) and electroencephalography (EEG), have improved rehabilitation results but still face challenges because of their inability to maintain reliable performance during user exhaustion and difficulties operating in challenging situations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has recently become a new neuroimaging technique that provides excellent imaging capability, can be used while moving, and has portable design features. fNIRS-based devices such as wheelchairs, robotic prostheses, and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have proven their ability to decode user intention and assist rehabilitation. The limited ability of fNIRS to measure time intervals prevents its use in real-time systems. The hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems combine EEG technology, which provides high-speed temporal measurements, with fNIRS technology, which provides spatial and hemodynamic measurements. The multimodal techniques combine different measurement methods, which improve accuracy while decreasing false positive results and increasing system adaptability. This review critically examines how AT control modalities have been evolving, and it also measures what fNIRS can do technically, plus what it struggles with, and then it pulls together the available evidence on hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems as a possible way toward more adaptive, user-centered rehabilitation technologies.

papers.title: Identification of Hypoxia- and Circadian Rhythm-Related Prognostic Genes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through Integrative Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analysis.
papers.abstract: Hypoxia perturbs circadian rhythm gene expression in hepatocellular carcinoma, yet prognostic genes associated with both processes remain insufficiently characterized. Data from the liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) cohort in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed. Candidate genes were identified by intersecting differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with 27 hypoxia- and circadian rhythm-related genes and were further refined using univariate Cox regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression; a random survival forest (RSF) risk model was then constructed and validated. Independent prognostic and functional enrichment analyses, immune infiltration profiling, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were subsequently performed. Four prognostic genes (ADM, PFKFB3, SERPINE1, and RORA) were identified through integrative computational analysis. The RSF model stratified LIHC patients into the high-risk group (HRG) and the low-risk group (LRG), which had significantly different survival outcomes, and the risk score and tumor stage were combined in a nomogram. The four genes were co-enriched in four pathways; eight immune cell types, including natural killer T (NKT) cells, differed between the risk groups. scRNA-seq identified stem-like/hypoxic malignant cells whose differentiation trajectory showed distinct expression dynamics of the four genes. IHC confirmed significantly higher ADM and PFKFB3 protein expression in LIHC tissues, whereas protein-level evidence for SERPINE1 and RORA was inconclusive. These findings support further prognostic evaluation of LIHC and investigation of the links among hypoxia, metabolic reprogramming, and stemness.

papers.title: Decision-Aligned Value Learning for Selective Adoption of EEG Fusion in Human-Robot Collaboration
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.

papers.title: Depression is associated with endometrial polyp occurrence and convergent gut microbiota-mitochondrial alterations: a multi-omics case-control study.
papers.abstract: Endometrial polyps (EPs) affect 7.8%-34.9% of women and cause abnormal uterine bleeding and reproductive failure, yet their pathogenesis is unclear. Depression is over-represented among women with EPs but is usually read as reactive distress; whether that association involves the gut microbiota and mitochondrial biology is unknown. We combined a hospital-based case-control analysis (n = 466), faecal full-length 16S rRNA and blood leukocyte RNA-seq in 30 participants (PD n = 11, PND n = 12, NPND n = 7), and a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model with bacterial supplementation. Depression was significantly associated with higher odds of EP in the full cohort (unadjusted OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.55-3.34; P < 0.001), and this trend remained stable following confounder adjustment, propensity-score matching and multiple sensitivity analyses. Signals were partitioned into EP-specific, depression-specific and dual-associated classes. In the EP-specific class, predicted microbial functions showed less electron-transfer gene content (complexes I-II), while host ETC subunits spanning complexes I, III and IV (NDUFA1, UQCRH, COX6B1, COX7A2) were coordinately downregulated and CCR2, CCR5 and UMPS upregulated, with enrichment for oxidative phosphorylation. Dual-associated signals comprised higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and lower Eggerthella lenta, negatively correlated (Kendall τ = -0.37, P = 0.007; PD > PND > NPND), together with downregulation of GDF15, HIC1, TCF7L2 and ICAM1. These findings place a convergent gut microbiota-mitochondrial axis at the intersection of depression and endometrial proliferation, and nominate candidate taxa and transcripts for hypothesis-driven validation. The axis proposed here is therefore hypothesis-generating and requires longitudinal, metabolomic and tissue-specific validation.
